title: Fix rate limiter owner attribution after API key transfer between workspaces
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: We are seeing intermittent misattribution of rate-limit and quota ownership when customers use the API key transfer / reassignment flow between workspaces (suborg transfer and admin-driven key reassignments). Symptoms include: users in the receiving workspace being blocked by rate limits that should be enforced on the source workspace, and usage being billed to the wrong workspace for a short window (minutes to hours).

What happens: The ingress path writes usage events and checks quotas against a cached token->owner mapping. When an API key is transferred, two things can happen concurrently: (1) the token mapping in the identity service is updated, and (2) the rate-limiter & billing caches are asynchronously invalidated. Race windows occur where requests still carry the old token mapping in rate-limiter caches while the identity service reports the new owner to the billing pipeline. This leads to requests counted against the old quota but billed to the new workspace (or vice versa) and occasional double-applied quota checks.

Scope: From our sampling and Grafana dashboard, ~0.8% of token-transfer events in the last 7 days produced at least one misattributed event; exfiltrated billing deltas observed range up to several hundred USD for affected customers in that period. A small set (~12) of customers opened support tickets.

Root cause hypothesis: Non-atomic transfer path combined with different consistency windows for (a) ingress rate-limiter caches, (b) realtime billing stream enrichment, and (c) downstream attribution in the billing ledger. The rate-limiter uses an in-memory token->bucket cache keyed by token_id but doesn't validate owner at enforcement time against the canonical identity service when transfers are recent.

Repro steps (dev):
1) Create two test workspaces A and B with low rate limits (5 req/min).
2) Issue API key K in workspace A; send steady requests -> observe rate-limiter bucket for A.
3) Use transfer API to reassign K to workspace B while continuing requests at ~2 req/sec.
4) Observe logs in ingress and rate-limiter: some requests are enforced against A's bucket while the billing stream enrichment shows owner=B for the same request IDs.

Proposed fix:
1) Short-term (mitigation): Add a synchronous owner-verify lookup in the rate-limiter for tokens whose last-transfer timestamp < 10 minutes. This is feature-flag guarded and adds a small lookup cost but eliminates the race window. Roll this to a small canary (10% of transfer traffic) first.
2) Medium-term (correctness): Implement an atomic transfer operation that writes a transfer record and increments a monotonic generation id for token->owner mapping. All caches must include generation id; enforcers should compare cached gen with identity service and fetch a miss on mismatch.
3) Billing pipeline: Emit transfer markers into the realtime usage stream so the ledger can attribute in-flight events to the correct owner or mark them for small-window backfill reconciliation. Add a ledger backfill job to reassign events in the window between transfer and cache-stabilization (default 1 hour).
4) Add alerting + dashboards: track percent of requests where enforcement_owner != billing_owner and broken_quota_events per transfer. Target remediation threshold <0.01%.

Acceptance criteria:
- No customer reports of incorrect quota enforcement after canary (10% then 50% then 100%).
- Misattribution metric (enforcement_owner != billing_owner) reduced to <0.01% in production for 48h after full rollout.
- Backfill job completes and reassigns >95% of misattributed events for the 7-day window prior to the fix.
- End-to-end tests that simulate high-concurrency transfers with consistent passes in CI.

Rollout plan:
- Day 0: Enable short-term mitigation behind FF for 10% of traffic, monitor.
- Day 1-2: Expand to 50% if metrics stable, run backfill on last 24h.
- Day 3: Full rollout and backfill 7 days.

Notes: This touches identity, rate-limiter, RPC caches, and billing enrichment. Coordinate with @Liang Zhou (identity) and @Sofia Martín (billing pipeline) for contract changes and schema for transfer markers.
comments: 2026-03-08 | Aisha Patel: Created ticket after support batch alerted on three customers and initial triage. Attached Grafana snapshots and example request ids. Marked P0 due to billing exposure.

2026-03-09 | Miguel Santos: Reproduced locally with synthetic transfer script. Confirmed race between in-memory rate-limiter cache and identity update. Drafted short-term verify patch in rate-limiter; needs perf check.
2026-03-10 | Liang Zhou: Identity team will add generation id to token records. We'll expose a light-weight endpoint to fetch (owner, generation) for a token. Expected ETA: 2026-03-16.
2026-03-11 | Sofia Martín: Billing will emit transfer markers in the realtime stream (PR #6223). We'll add enrichment to tag events with transfer-gen when available.

2026-03-12 | Miguel Santos: Implemented FF-gated sync-verify in rate-limiter (branch: eng/ENG-20488-sync-verify). Initial perf microbench shows ~5% p50 latency increase under synthetic load; acceptable for 10% rollout.
2026-03-13 | Support (Maya Chen): Notified affected customers that we are working on attribution fixes and have queued a backfill for billing adjustments if needed.

2026-03-14 | Miguel Santos: Canary rollout to 10% started at 09:30 UTC. Monitoring enforcement_owner != billing_owner metric and rate-limit latency. No regressions observed in first 24h. Planning expansion after identity generation endpoint is available.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Canary shows no increase in customer-facing rate-limit errors. 2) Misattribution metric <0.01% for 48h after full rollout. 3) Backfill job reassigns >95% of misattributed events in the 7-day window. 4) Unit and integration tests added; cross-team schema changes documented and signed off.
customer_notes: We will proactively adjust any incorrectly billed usage discovered during the backfill and notify affected customers via support. Short-term mitigation reduces risk of new misattribution while we complete the atomic transfer design.
